answer:
**Raise standard pricing to $500, then sell five premium places at $2,500—not $2,000. Defer the course.** Validate premium demand before reducing your client roster.

The constraint is hours. At $500, your existing book produces $20,700 monthly profit. Five premium upgrades add ten weekly hours, so you must release ten other standard clients. At your proposed $2,000 premium price, that leaves only $23,600 profit.

At $2,500, the steady-state plan works:

| Clients | Monthly revenue | Weekly delivery hours |
|---|---:|---:|
| 30 standard | $15,000 | 30 |
| 5 premium | $12,500 | 15 |
| Admin | — | 5 |
| **Total** | **$27,500** | **50** |

Subtract $1,400 in client costs: **$26,100 monthly profit**, before personal taxes and assuming premium adds no software costs.

Premium should include standard bookkeeping plus:

- A rolling 13-week cash forecast, refreshed weekly using agreed inputs.
- Monthly inventory purchasing recommendations tied to cash, stock levels and supplier lead times.
- One monthly planning meeting.
- Tax-preparer coordination using reconciled reports and an agreed request list.

Cap additional work at two hours weekly per premium client. Define response times and required client inputs; exclude purchasing execution, tax preparation and unlimited advisory requests.

Give pricing notice now and offer the package to your eight larger clients. Secure paid commitments, then stagger transitions: each upgrade requires releasing two other standard clients first. Complete this over months three through six.

The table leaves no spare capacity. For two hours of weekly headroom, retain only 28 standard clients; profit becomes $25,180. Prefer that operating target once setup is complete. If five clients will not buy at $2,500, revisit pricing or scope before offboarding. The course adds production and marketing work without established demand.
